concepts.name: Standardised Weights and Measures System
key_dimensions: Binary and decimal progression of weights (1, 2, 4, 8, 16... and 10, 20, 40...)
Material used: chert/jasper cuboid weights — absence of metal weights
Uniformity across geographically distant sites implying centralised regulation
Contrast with contemporary Mesopotamian and Egyptian weight systems — UPSC trap: IVC had no known standard ruler equivalent until the ivory scale at Lothal

concepts.name: Bead-Making Technology and Trade
key_dimensions: Materials used: carnelian, lapis lazuli, steatite, faience, gold, shell, terracotta — site-specific sourcing
Specialized drill technology: use of Ernestite (a hard stone) micro-drills for long barrel carnelian beads — unique to IVC
Bead-making workshop evidence at Chanhudaro and Lothal — distinction between the two sites
Export of beads to Mesopotamia as evidence of long-distance trade — trap: lapis lazuli was imported INTO IVC from Badakhshan (Afghanistan), not exported

concepts.name: Pottery: Wheel-Thrown and Kiln-Fired Techniques
key_dimensions: Use of fast potter's wheel — technological advancement over preceding Neolithic cultures
Distinctive black-on-red painted pottery with geometric and natural motifs
Perforated pottery (strainer jars) and their possible functional uses
Distinction between Harappan pottery and Painted Grey Ware (PGW) of later Vedic period — common UPSC confusion point

concepts.name: Bronze and Copper Metallurgy
key_dimensions: Use of lost-wax (cire perdue) casting technique — evidenced by the Dancing Girl of Mohenjo-daro
Tin-bronze alloy composition — tin sourced possibly from Afghanistan/Central Asia, implying trade networks
Copper sourced from Khetri mines (Rajasthan) — site-specific knowledge
Absence of iron technology — critical UPSC trap: IVC is a Bronze Age civilisation; iron appears only in later Vedic/PGW phase

concepts.name: Faience and Glazed Steatite Technology
key_dimensions: Faience: man-made vitreous material (quartz/sand + alkali + colourant) — one of earliest synthetic materials
Use in beads, seals, small figurines and amulets
Fired steatite (soapstone) for seal-making: softness before firing, hardness after — deliberate technological exploitation
Parallel development of faience in Egypt and Mesopotamia — IVC faience considered independently developed or diffused (contested scholarly debate)

concepts.name: Seal-Making Craft and Iconography
key_dimensions: Material: predominantly steatite; also copper, terracotta, ivory seals found
Unicorn as the most common animal motif — UPSC trap: unicorn ≠ horse; horse is notably absent from IVC seals
Pashupati seal from Mohenjo-daro: proto-Shiva debate — functional vs. religious interpretation
Seals' administrative/commercial function: perforated boss on reverse for string attachment — evidence of mercantile use

concepts.name: Textile Production: Cotton and Weaving
key_dimensions: Earliest evidence of cotton cultivation and use in the world — IVC credited with domesticating Gossypium arboreum
Indirect evidence: spindle whorls, needle fragments, impression on silver vase at Mohenjo-daro
No direct textile finds due to preservation issues — trap: absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence
Contrast: Mesopotamian textiles were predominantly wool; IVC's cotton specialisation as a distinguishing feature

concepts.name: Shell-Working Industry
key_dimensions: Turbinella pyrum (sacred chank) shell used for bangles, ladles, inlay work
Shell-working workshops identified at Nageshwar and Balakot (coastal sites) — raw material procurement logic
Finished shell objects found inland at Harappa and Mohenjo-daro — evidence of inter-regional exchange within IVC
Trap: Shell objects were luxury/ritual items, not everyday utilities — informs social stratification debates

concepts.name: Town Planning as Technological Achievement: Grid Layout and Drainage
key_dimensions: Orthogonal (grid-iron) street planning with streets aligned cardinal directions
Underground covered brick drainage system — unique in the ancient world; no contemporary parallel in Egypt/Mesopotamia
Standardised burnt brick ratio (1:2:4) used consistently across sites — implies centralised knowledge or authority
Trap: Not all IVC sites had identical planning — Dholavira had unique water reservoir system; Lothal had a tidal dockyard — site-specific exceptions

concepts.name: Dockyard and Maritime Technology at Lothal
key_dimensions: Lothal's trapezoidal basin interpreted as the world's earliest tidal dockyard by S.R. Rao — contested by later scholars (some argue it was a water reservoir)
Orientation of the basin aligned with prevailing tidal flow of Bhogavo river
Evidence of sea trade: Persian Gulf seals, Mesopotamian cylinder seal found at Lothal
Trap: Lothal is in Gujarat (Saurashtra region) on the Bhogavo river — frequently confused with Rangpur or Surkotada in exam options

concepts.name: Water Management and Reservoir Technology
key_dimensions: Dholavira's sophisticated water harvesting system: 16+ reservoirs carved into rock — most elaborate water system in IVC
Stepwells (vav precursors) at Mohenjo-daro and other sites
The Great Bath of Mohenjo-daro: waterproofing technique using bitumen lining and burnt bricks with gypsum mortar
Trap: Great Bath's purpose is debated — ritual purification vs. public bathing vs. administrative control; UPSC often tests the 'most accepted' interpretation

concepts.name: Terracotta Craft: Figurines, Toys, and Brick-Making
key_dimensions: Mother Goddess figurines: hand-modelled, not wheel-thrown — interpreted as fertility/religious objects
Animal figurines and wheeled toy carts — evidence of concept of wheel in transportation
Standardised brick sizes across sites as evidence of advanced knowledge of ratios and construction planning
Trap: Terracotta figurines are abundant but script on them is rare — contrast with seals which combine image AND script

concepts.name: Ivory Working
key_dimensions: Ivory used for combs, rods, inlay, and measuring scale (Lothal ivory scale)
Lothal ivory scale: smallest division ~1.7mm — remarkable precision suggesting advanced measurement needs
Elephant domestication debated — wild elephant hunting vs. domestication for ivory procurement
Trap: Ivory scale at Lothal is significant as it represents a LINEAR measure — complements the cuboid weight system (mass measure) at other sites

concepts.name: Gold and Silver Craftsmanship
key_dimensions: Granulation technique on gold jewellery — evidence of high craft specialisation
Sources of gold debated: Karnataka (Kolar), Afghanistan — implies long-distance procurement
Silver more abundant than gold in IVC — contrast with Egyptian preference for gold
Hoards of jewellery (e.g., Allahdino hoard) suggest concepts of wealth storage and possibly private property

concepts.name: Indus Script as a Craft/Technological Artefact
key_dimensions: Script appears primarily on seals, tablets, pottery — functional rather than literary/monumental use
Undeciphered status: ~400-600 signs identified — neither purely alphabetic nor purely pictographic (debated)
Absence of bilingual inscription (unlike Rosetta Stone) as key obstacle to decipherment
Trap: Indus script direction is right-to-left (boustrophedon in some cases) — UPSC sometimes tests directionality; also trap: no Indus script found on monumental architecture

concepts.name: Craft Specialisation and Evidence of Division of Labour
key_dimensions: Distinct craft quarters/workshops identified archaeologically at Chanhudaro (bead + seal making), Lothal (bead making + dockyard)
Absence of temples or palaces — craft production possibly state/elite controlled without religious institutional framework (contrast with Mesopotamia)
Variation in house sizes at Mohenjo-daro indicating social stratification linked to craft/trade prosperity
Trap: Unlike Mesopotamia and Egypt, no written records of craft guilds or labour organisation — inferences are purely archaeological

concepts.name: Absence of Certain Technologies: Horses, Iron, and Monumental Script
key_dimensions: Horse bones absent from IVC sites (debated — Surkotada claimed horse bones but contested by scholars)
No iron technology — IVC remains exclusively Chalcolithic/Bronze Age
No monumental inscriptions or royal proclamations — contrast with contemporary Mesopotamian and Egyptian civilisations
UPSC trap: These absences are frequently used in questions to test knowledge of what IVC did NOT have — 'which of the following is NOT associated with IVC' type questions

concepts.name: Inter-Regional Raw Material Procurement Networks
key_dimensions: Lapis lazuli from Badakhshan (Afghanistan); tin from Afghanistan/Central Asia; copper from Khetri (Rajasthan); chert from Rohri Hills (Sindh)
Presence of Harappan outposts at Shortugai (Afghanistan) — possibly for lapis lazuli procurement
Gulf of Khambhat (Cambay) region for carnelian — Lothal as processing centre
Trap: Raw material sourcing geography directly informs questions on IVC trade routes and the geographic extent of IVC interaction sphere

concepts.name: Technological Decline Theories and Craft Evidence
key_dimensions: Late Harappan phase shows deterioration in craft quality: smaller seals, cruder pottery, standardisation breakdown
Possible causes: ecological degradation, trade network collapse, tectonic activity (Dholavira water system abandonment)
Continuity of some crafts (bead-making, pottery) into post-urban Chalcolithic cultures of Deccan
Trap: Decline was gradual and regional, NOT simultaneous — eastern sites (Rakhigarhi, Kalibangan) declined earlier while some western sites persisted longer
